A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same masked-diffusion HMER work, renamed GryphOne in v2. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison. Both were inspected through their references; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original MathWriting and CROHME evaluations, component ablations, inference measurements and output-diversity analyses in Tables 1–4 and Figures 6–7.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and ablations, plus refinement trajectories, structural-error recovery and accuracy–latency experiments in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–6.

M1.justification: The core encoder–decoder, SAT and RMML remain. Algorithm 2 makes a limited procedural correction: v1 remasks predictions at time t, whereas v2 explicitly predicts the clean sequence and remasks at t−1, leaving the final output unmasked. Expanded architecture and loss descriptions otherwise primarily disclose existing components.

E1.justification: MathWriting and CROHME 2014/2016/2019/2023 remain the benchmark coverage. v2 Section 4.9 adds a distinct recovery scenario initialized with operator-deleted expressions, extending evaluation from recognition from fully masked sequences to correction of partially corrupted symbolic inputs.

E2.justification: v2 adds matched TAMER and PosFormer comparisons on both benchmarks, Mask-Predict decoding on MathWriting, and literature-only NAMER scores on CROHME. It removes CTC, PaLI and PaLIGemma from MathWriting and replaces the extensive literature-comparison block on CROHME. BTTR, CoMER, ICAL and Google OCR, renamed OCR, remain.

E3.justification: The main training dataset, held-out CROHME evaluation, rasterization and core metrics remain. v2 expands the latency study from T={2,10,50} to {1,2,5,10,20,50} and introduces timestep-controlled recovery tests that retain arguments and braces while removing operators. Reported near-match thresholds are reduced to ≤1 rather than including ≤2 and CROHME 2023's ≤3/≤4.

E4.justification: v2 adds an RMML-only control, step-wise CER/EM/SER trajectories and targeted structural-error recovery, and expands latency and diversity analyses. These substantially strengthen investigation of component effects and refinement behavior. Conversely, v1's test-set component-ablation table and two of its three qualitative cases are removed.

E5.justification: v1 specifies ten-run averaging for Proposal in the main comparison captions. v2 Section 4.1 explicitly extends the statement to all results and identifies these as inference runs. This broadens reporting without establishing additional training runs; neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests or seed-based uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Proposed-method scores, ablations and throughput are extensively revised, with additional diagnostic results. MathWriting's headline changes from 5.56% CER/60.42% EM for SAT-only Proposal to 5.51%/59.9% for GryphOne with RMML; v1's corresponding RMML row reports 5.55%/59.60%. Reported T=50 throughput changes from 0.62 to 21.2 FPS, but v1 lacks hardware details needed to establish a comparable speedup.

T1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects the reverse-time specification by remasking at t−1 instead of t, ensuring zero masking at termination. The newly written embedding sum, expanded two-view loss and factorized corruption equation otherwise formalize operations already described in v1. No theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central diffusion, SAT and RMML contributions remain. v2 narrows broad state-of-the-art claims to superiority over reimplemented baselines under matched conditions and explicitly claims the first application of masked diffusion to HMER. Its abstract also more clearly identifies CROHME as held-out cross-dataset evaluation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning repeated-pass latency, dependence on large training datasets and fixed-resolution inputs. New analyses interpret complementary SAT/RMML effects, refinement convergence and recovery failures at intermediate timesteps, including higher recovery CER with SAT despite improved SER. These substantially expand the account of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies PyTorch/DINO, encoder dimensions, decoder depth, attention heads, dropout, sequence padding, epochs, batch size, AdamW settings and V100 timing hardware. It also details modifier alignment and loss computation over masked and unmasked positions. These are primarily disclosures, not demonstrated setting changes. Conversely, v1's explicit 626K training count and parameter-count columns disappear.

R1.justification: v2 adds explicit positioning against confidence-guided Mask-Predict and references for DINO, AdamW and Transformers. It removes the large-scale-data subsection and references to PaLI, PaLIGemma, MMHMER, Tex80M and Sahoo et al.'s masked diffusion work. Most of the HMER research lineage and its relationship to AR, NAR and syntax-aware models remain.

P1.justification: Beyond naming the method GryphOne, v2 extensively rewrites existing prose, moves related work before methodology, separates training and inference explanations, and organizes components into Method/Effect discussions. Experimental reporting is reorganized into substantially more focused subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Architecture/refinement and SAT illustrations are substantially redrawn, the separate RMML diagram is removed, and new trajectory/recovery plots appear. CROHME tables are merged, benchmark columns are streamlined, and component ablations and latency results receive separate displays.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility through previously missing implementation and training specifications. Mask-Predict comparisons, an RMML-only control and targeted refinement analyses provide stronger evidence for the central mechanism, while matched-setting claims and explicit limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of test-set component ablations and some broader comparisons. The large throughput revisions remain insufficiently explained for cross-version speed claims.
